query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Wear performance in high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is primarily governed by local lattice distortion that impedes dislocation activity, reducing both plastic deformation and crack initiation under frictional stresses.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline equiatomic HEA coating (e.g., a quinary alloy) produced via sputter-deposition and annealed under identical conditions, with minimal secondary phases or grain-boundary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with 2–5 at.% of a larger or smaller atomic-radius element (e.g., Hf or Nb) to increase local lattice distortion while keeping other parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Assess wear under a standardized dry-sliding or pin-on-disk test at moderate loads (e.g., up to ~80 N) and ambient temperature, using the same counterface material and surface finish.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local lattice distortion (and any associated microstructural changes) that can be tracked via X-ray or neutron diffraction, as well as electron microscopy.
generation.mechanism: Greater lattice distortion from doping elevates the strain field and hinders dislocation movement, which in turn reduces crack nucleation and material removal during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the undoped baseline, the doped samples should exhibit a measurably lower wear rate (on the order of ~20–40% reduction) and reduced friction coefficient under otherwise identical test conditions.
generation.baseline: An undoped high-entropy alloy coating composition without the added element, processed under identical conditions (same substrate, deposition method, annealing profile).
generation.boundary: This effect should hold at moderate temperatures (below major phase transformation points) and normal loads where plastic deformation is a contributing wear mechanism; very high temperatures, severe oxidation, or different wear modes might invalidate the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of performance improvement can vary depending on processing history and the specific doping element. If secondary phase formation occurs, it may overshadow the lattice distortion effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Systematically fabricate a series of HEA coatings with 0%, 2%, and 5% doping of the selected element. Characterize microstructure for lattice distortion (via X-ray diffraction peak shifts, electron microscopy). Conduct identical pin-on-disk wear tests, measuring coefficient of friction and wear volume/loss.
measurements: Changes in lattice parameter and peak broadening in XRD
Wear track depth and volume loss from 3D surface profilometry
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If wear rates do not improve in parallel with measured increases in lattice distortion (or if increased distortion simply worsens wear performance), the local lattice-distortion mechanism is invalidated.
